items.title: Why We Preach Fearlessly
items.answer:
Brothers and sisters, imagine being given a speaking assignment where the audience is guaranteed to be difficult. They will not want to hear you. They may mock you. Some may even threaten you. Now imagine doing that for years. That, in effect, was Ezekiel’s assignment. Jehovah sent him to preach to his own countrymen — people whose hearts were set against the message. But notice how Jehovah prepared him. Before Ezekiel went, God said: “I have made your forehead like a diamond, harder than flint. Do not be afraid of them or be terrified by their faces.” (Eze 3:9) Think about that. The command not to be afraid is repeated to Ezekiel again and again in these opening chapters — Jehovah knew Ezekiel felt the weight of the assignment.

Do we feel the weight today? We preach in a world that is largely indifferent. Many who hear us are, in their own way, “hardheaded and hardhearted” (Eze 3:7). Some ridicule; some react angrily. And yet this is the very work in which we need to be fearless. This week’s reading — Ezekiel 3 and 4 — gives us three solid reasons to preach fearlessly: where our strength comes from, whose message we carry, and what our work is accomplishing.

OUR STRENGTH AND SUPPORT COME FROM JEHOVAH

Ezekiel’s courage was not self-generated. Listen to verse 8: “Look! I have made your face exactly as hard as their faces and your forehead exactly as hard as their foreheads.” (Eze 3:8) Notice who did the making — “I have made.” Jehovah himself equipped Ezekiel for the hardness of the assignment before Ezekiel ever faced it. And he does the same for us (w22.11 5 ¶¶10-11). Not by making our faces physically hard — in ways just as real. Through prayer: courage grows every time we ask for it and receive it. Through his spirit: the same force that strengthened Ezekiel strengthens us as we preach. And through the congregation: a companion in the ministry, an encouraging word after a hard morning, a family that prays with us before we go out.

Has that been your experience? Imagine a publisher who trembles at the thought of one particular door — she knows the face behind it has been unfriendly before. She prays right there on the step — not for an easy audience, but for courage to speak — and she finds her voice. That is not coincidence. That is what “I have made your face … hard” looks like in our day. When fear whispers that we are too weak, the honest answer is: we are — on our own. But Jehovah never sends us out on our own. He who sends also supplies.

So the question is not whether we will feel fear — Ezekiel surely did; Jehovah told him three times not to be afraid. The question is where we take that fear. If we carry it alone, it grows heavier every week. But if we hand it to Jehovah in prayer before every witnessing shift, he replaces it with a strength that is not our own — the strength of the One who says, “I have made.”

OUR MESSAGE IS FROM JEHOVAH

Second, Ezekiel could be fearless because the message was not his. Before he went, Jehovah had him eat the scroll — internalize it — and then said: “Son of man, take to heart and listen to all my words that I speak to you.” (Eze 3:10) Then: “Go in among the exiles of your people and speak to them. Tell them, ‘This is what the Sovereign Lord Jehovah says,’ whether they listen or refuse to listen.” (Eze 3:11) Notice those last words — “whether they listen or refuse to listen.” Ezekiel’s success was not measured by results; it was measured by faithfulness. And what gave his words weight? Not his eloquence, but their Source.

The Bible-teaching book makes the same point for us (bt 134 ¶7): our message is Jehovah’s — we are messengers, not originators. That reality changes how we feel about rejection. If someone shuts a door on me, what are they really rejecting? Not my personal opinions — I am simply delivering a decree that was written long before I was born. And it changes how we prepare. A messenger who mumbles the King’s decree brings embarrassment on himself; a messenger who has taken the words to heart speaks with quiet conviction. So we do well to ask: Have I “eaten the scroll” — studied it, meditated on it, made the message my own? The more the message is in us, the less we depend on our own ability, and the more fearless we become. Jehovah is speaking through his Word today. We simply open our mouths and let it be heard.

OUR EFFORTS ARE LIFESAVING

Third — and this is the reason that steadies us on the hardest mornings — our efforts are lifesaving. Jehovah told Ezekiel plainly: “When I say to someone wicked, ‘You will surely die,’ but you do not warn him … he will die for his error because he is wicked, but I will ask his blood back from you.” And on the other side: “if you warn someone wicked and he does not turn back from his wickedness … he will die for his error, but you will certainly save your own life.” (Eze 3:18, 19) There it is — bloodguilt. Not because Ezekiel could force anyone to change, but because a watchman who sees the danger and stays silent shares responsibility for the outcome.

How does that touch us? Through Paul’s counsel to Timothy: “Pay constant attention to yourself and to your teaching. Persevere in these things, for by doing this you will save both yourself and those who listen to you.” (1 Tim. 4:16) Notice — “both yourself and those who listen.” Our own salvation is tied up in the warning work. And the Watchtower of May 2018 reminds us that we cannot tell who will respond (w18.05 19 ¶¶8-9): the meek, righteous-hearted people are scattered among all kinds of neighbors. Some will be saved from destruction simply because a publisher knocked, or waited, or came back a third time. Every return visit we make, every letter we write, every conversation at the cart could be the warning that saves a life. When we see our ministry that way, fear shrinks to its true size. What is a red face at one more unfriendly door, compared with being the instrument that helps pull a neighbor out of the fire?

And notice how personal this responsibility is. Jehovah said to Ezekiel: “you will certainly save your own life.” Our perseverance in the preaching work is part of our own salvation. That truth made fearless preachers out of people far more timid than any of us — and it can do the same for us.

CONCLUSION

So — why do we preach fearlessly? Because of who equips us: Jehovah himself has made us able. Because of whose message it is: the Sovereign Lord Jehovah’s, not ours — so our success is measured by faithfulness, not by results. And because of what is at stake: lives — theirs, and our own. Ezekiel’s audience never got easier; the hardness stayed right to the end of his ministry. But the man who had eaten the scroll went where he was sent, said what he was given, and Jehovah carried him through. Our audience will not get easier either — the days are growing harder and the warning work more urgent. But we can go out this week the way Ezekiel went out: forehead like flint — not because we are naturally bold, but because the One who sent us has already equipped us, the message is his, and the work is lifesaving. May each of us preach fearlessly, and find, as Ezekiel did, that Jehovah is with us every step of the way.

scriptures.quote: I have made your forehead like a diamond, harder than flint. Do not be afraid of them or be terrified by their faces, for they are a rebellious house.”
But the house of Israel will refuse to listen to you, for they do not want to listen to me. All those of the house of Israel are hardheaded and hardhearted.
Look! I have made your face exactly as hard as their faces and your forehead exactly as hard as their foreheads.
He went on to say to me: “Son of man, take to heart and listen to all my words that I speak to you.
Go in among the exiles of your people and speak to them. Tell them, ‘This is what the Sovereign Lord Jehovah says,’ whether they listen or refuse to listen.”

When I say to someone wicked, ‘You will surely die,’ but you do not warn him, and you fail to speak in order to warn the wicked one to turn from his wicked course so that he may stay alive, he will die for his error because he is wicked, but I will ask his blood back from you.
But if you warn someone wicked and he does not turn back from his wickedness and from his wicked course, he will die for his error, but you will certainly save your own life.
Pay constant attention to yourself and to your teaching. Persevere in these things, for by doing this you will save both yourself and those who listen to you.

items.title: Spiritual Gems
items.answer:
What I learned from this week’s Bible reading (Ezekiel 3-4):

1. Jehovah listens to the honest concerns of his servants. Ezekiel protested the revolting fuel he was told to bake his bread over: “Not that, Sovereign Lord Jehovah! From my youth until now, I have not been defiled …” (Eze 4:14) And Jehovah did not rebuke him — he adjusted: “All right, I will allow you to use cattle manure instead of human excrement.” (Eze 4:15) The Sovereign Lord of the universe listened to an objection about fuel. He is not offended by sincere questions or honest concerns — he answers them.

2. Being a watchman is a serious responsibility. “Son of man, I have appointed you as a watchman to the house of Israel.” (Eze 3:17) If the watchman stays silent, Jehovah says: “I will ask his blood back from you” (Eze 3:18). We cannot know who will listen, so we cannot afford to stay silent.

3. Before we speak for Jehovah, we must take in his words. “Son of man, take to heart and listen to all my words that I speak to you.” (Eze 3:10) Ezekiel had to eat the scroll before he could declare it. Preaching flows from personal study — nothing goes out from the heart that has not first gone in.

Practical examples from these scriptures — how they have helped, or can help:
• Eze 4:14, 15 helped me personally: when I struggled to accept something I was taught, I prayed about it honestly and researched it carefully instead of quietly drifting away. Finding the solid reasons myself settled my heart far more firmly than never having questioned would have.
• Eze 3:17, 18 helps me at work and in the family: when a workmate or relative is heading into real harm — a reckless decision, a course that is destroying him — this moves me to say something kindly but clearly, instead of staying silent to keep the peace.
• Eze 3:10 shapes my preparation for the ministry: before going out, I read the day’s text and the week’s reading and pick one thought to take to heart — so that what I say at the door comes from the heart, not from a memorized presentation.

scriptures.quote: I then said: “Not that, Sovereign Lord Jehovah! From my youth until now, I have not been defiled by eating meat from an animal found dead or a torn animal, and no unclean meat has entered my mouth.”
So he said to me: “All right, I will allow you to use cattle manure instead of human excrement, and you will bake your bread over it.”
“Son of man, I have appointed you as a watchman to the house of Israel; and when you hear a word from my mouth, you must warn them from me.

When I say to someone wicked, ‘You will surely die,’ but you do not warn him, and you fail to speak in order to warn the wicked one to turn from his wicked course so that he may stay alive, he will die for his error because he is wicked, but I will ask his blood back from you.
He went on to say to me: “Son of man, take to heart and listen to all my words that I speak to you.

items.title: Bible Reading — Eze 3:16-27 (th study 2)
items.answer:
Context: Jehovah appoints Ezekiel as watchman over the exiles — responsible to warn the wicked and the righteous alike; then Jehovah restrains him, making him as one bound and mute except when speaking Jehovah’s word, until the time comes to speak.

Lesson 1: The warning work carries responsibility on both sides — the watchman must speak, and the hearer must respond (Eze 3:18, 19, 21). Lesson 2: Jehovah’s servants speak when and what Jehovah wants — the message and the timing belong to him (Eze 3:26, 27).

Possible comment: “But if you have warned the righteous one not to sin, and he does not sin, he will surely keep alive because he was warned, and you will have saved your own life.” (Eze 3:21) Reading this reminds me that warnings save lives — including our own. When we lovingly warn a brother who is drifting, we may help rescue him; and our own faithfulness is preserved precisely by speaking.

scriptures.quote: But if you have warned the righteous one not to sin, and he does not sin, he will surely keep alive because he was warned, and you will have saved your own life.”

items.title: Starting a Conversation — House to House (lmd lesson 1 point 5)
items.answer:
lmd lesson 1 point 5 — “Listen. Don’t talk too much. Encourage the other person to express himself. When appropriate, ask questions.”

HOUSE TO HOUSE — Daniel shares one Bible truth from appendix A of the Love People brochure (truth 30: “Dead loved ones will be resurrected”) and then, true to the point, stops talking: a short opener, one scripture, and questions that let Ruth express herself.

Daniel (Publisher): “Good morning! I’m Daniel, from the local congregation. We’re speaking with neighbours briefly today. Can I ask you something? Have you ever lost someone you loved — someone you wish you could see again?”
Ruth (Householder): “Yes … my mother. Two years ago now.”
Daniel (Publisher): “I’m sorry, Ruth. That kind of loss never fully stops hurting, does it? You know, the Bible speaks about exactly that. Did you know that Jesus said the dead will actually come back to life — here on the earth?”
Ruth (Householder): “Really? The Bible says that?”
Daniel (Publisher): “It does — right here. ‘Do not be amazed at this, for the hour is coming in which all those in the memorial tombs will hear his voice and come out.’ (John 5:28, 29) But tell me — what would it mean to you to see your mother again, healthy and happy, on a peaceful earth?”
Ruth (Householder): “Honestly? That would be everything. I think about her every day.”
Daniel (Publisher): “Thank you for sharing that with me — really. Many of our neighbours feel the same way. May I leave this brochure with you? There’s a section in it about the resurrection. And could I come back next week? I’d love to hear more about your mother.”
Ruth (Householder): “Yes — please do come back.”

Keys: Daniel followed lmd lesson 1 point 5. He shared just one truth, then stopped talking: he asked what seeing her mother again would mean to Ruth, he listened, and he let her express her feelings. The seed is planted — and the next conversation is already arranged.

scriptures.quote: Do not be amazed at this, for the hour is coming in which all those in the memorial tombs will hear his voice and come out, those who did good things to a resurrection of life, and those who practiced vile things to a resurrection of judgment.

items.cite: lmd lesson 1 point 5; appendix A of the Love People brochure (truth 30)

items.title: Starting a Conversation — Public Witnessing (lmd lesson 4 point 4)
items.answer:
lmd lesson 4 point 4 — “Make clear that the Bible is the source of the truths you share. God’s Word contains thoughts that touch people’s hearts. When we use it, we are building their faith on the right foundation.”

PUBLIC WITNESSING — Ruth stops at the literature cart with an accusation she has heard. Daniel stays humble, does not argue, and lets the Bible itself answer.

Daniel (Publisher): “Good afternoon! We’re offering the magazines free of charge today.”
Ruth (Householder): “Oh — you’re the ones, aren’t you? I’ve heard you people are a cult. My cousin warned me about you.”
Daniel (Publisher): “That’s a fair question to raise, and I’m glad you said it to my face rather than just walking past. May I ask — when people say ‘cult,’ what do you understand by that?”
Ruth (Householder): “I suppose … a group that follows one leader blindly. And that doesn’t really use the Bible.”
Daniel (Publisher): “I understand the concern — sadly, some groups do fit that. But I don’t want you to take my word for anything. Let’s let the Bible answer. Jesus said his true followers would be known by something very specific. Here: ‘By this all will know that you are my disciples—if you have love among yourselves.’ (John 13:35) A cult doesn’t match that mark, does it? And notice — it’s the Bible doing the talking, not me. Why don’t you bring me a question of your own, and we’ll see what God’s Word says about it?”
Ruth (Householder): “Hm. I do have one, actually … why God allows so much suffering.”
Daniel (Publisher): “A question the Bible answers beautifully. Let’s look at it now — and if you’d like, we can continue at your home one evening this week. What suits you?”

Keys: Daniel carried out lmd lesson 4 point 4: instead of defending himself, he made the Bible the source of the truths he shared — he read John 13:35 with Ruth and invited her to test it with her own question. His humility (no argument, no insisting) gave God’s Word room to touch her heart on the right foundation.

scriptures.quote: Do nothing out of contentiousness or out of egotism, but with humility consider others superior to you,
I am giving you a new commandment, that you love one another; just as I have loved you, you also love one another. By this all will know that you are my disciples—if you have love among yourselves.

items.title: Making Disciples (lmd lesson 12 point 4)
items.answer:
lmd lesson 12 point 4 — “Identify obstacles to progress, and help your student overcome those obstacles. Ask yourself: ‘If my student is not progressing toward baptism, what is hindering him?’ ‘What practical help can I offer?’ Pray for the courage to discuss frankly and lovingly what your student needs to do.”

MAKING DISCIPLES — Daniel conducts the Bible study with Ruth, his student. Her progress has slowed, and the obstacle is cleanliness — her home has become cluttered and disorganized, her study preparations have slipped, and she feels ashamed to admit it. With the lesson’s principle in mind — “Oil and incense make the heart rejoice; so does sweet friendship springing from sincere counsel” (Prov. 27:9) — Daniel speaks frankly yet lovingly and offers practical help.

Daniel (Publisher): “Ruth, before we begin — your comment at the meeting on Sunday was excellent. You really are making progress. But can we talk honestly for a few minutes? I’ve noticed our study preparations have been difficult for a few weeks now.”
Ruth (Householder): “I know … honestly, Daniel, the house is such a mess. I can’t even find my Bible half the time, and by the time I’ve cleared a chair to sit on, I’m too tired to study.”
Daniel (Publisher): “Thank you for being honest with me — that helps me help you. You know, cleanliness and order matter to Jehovah; the Bible shows that our worship and our daily life go together. A clean, orderly home isn’t about impressing anyone — it gives you a calm place to meet with Jehovah and keeps your mind clear. Can we make it simple together? Each evening, just fifteen minutes to tidy the corner where we study — and the Bible and the study folder always go back to the same drawer. Could you try that this week?”
Ruth (Householder): “Fifteen minutes I can do. It’s the whole house that overwhelms me.”
Daniel (Publisher): “Then let’s not talk about the whole house — only this corner, and only this week. And here’s something practical: if a day goes wrong and it doesn’t happen, tell me at the study, and we’ll adjust the time — no embarrassment, no lectures. The goal isn’t a perfect house, Ruth. It’s a clear mind, a clean heart, and steady steps toward baptism — and you are far closer than you feel right now.”
Ruth (Householder): “Thank you for saying it straight but kindly. I’ll start tonight.”
Daniel (Publisher): “Good. And I’ll keep praying for you about it — as I’m sure you will for me; it takes courage to raise these things on both sides. Now — to today’s lesson.”

Keys: Daniel carried out lmd lesson 12 point 4. He identified the obstacle to progress — clutter and disorder that had buried Ruth’s Bible, her preparations and her enthusiasm. Praying for courage, he discussed cleanliness frankly but lovingly, offered practical help (a fifteen-minute routine, one fixed place for study materials, an agreed way to handle missed days), commended her progress, and set a short-term goal — exactly the sincere counsel that makes sweet friendship and keeps a student moving toward baptism.

scriptures.quote: Oil and incense make the heart rejoice; So does sweet friendship springing from sincere counsel.

items.title: Local Needs
items.answer: Congregation-specific talk. The subject of the Local Needs part is chosen by the body of elders to meet a specific need in the local congregation, so no prepared script can be written in advance. The speaker should obtain the topic and any sources from the elders and prepare accordingly — building the talk on the Scriptures, with practical, upbuilding direction that helps the congregation apply the counsel locally. (See the Ministry Ideas section of the workbook week for guidance on preparing this part.)

items.title: Congregation Bible Study — Walk Courageously With God, chap. 20
items.answer: Study source: the book Walk Courageously With God! (wcg), chapter 20, “He Found Courage in a Time of Weakness” — the account of Samson (wcg chap. 20 pp. 94-97). The Bible account read: Judges 13:1–16:31. Below are prepared answers to every question in the chapter — the discussion question, Dig Deeper, Reflect on the Lessons and Meditate on the Bigger Picture.

cbs.label: For discussion
cbs.q: In what ways did Samson show courage?
cbs.answer: Samson showed courage all his life. He faced a thousand armed Philistines alone, armed with nothing but the jawbone of a donkey. At midnight he tore up the gates of Gaza and carried them up a mountain. Blinded, mocked and enslaved, he still prayed for strength one last time and struck a final blow for Jehovah. And he showed a quieter courage: he faced his own failure honestly and turned back to Jehovah at the end. “Let me die with the Phi·lisʹtines!” he called — and won his greatest victory in death.

scriptures.quote: Samson called out: “Let me die with the Phi·lisʹtines!” Then he pushed with all his might, and the house fell on the lords and all the people in it. So he killed more at his death than he had killed during his life.

cbs.label: Dig Deeper · 1
cbs.q: Why could Samson touch dead bodies and still remain a Nazirite? (w05 1/15 30 ¶1–31 ¶1)
cbs.answer: The uncut hair was the visible symbol of Samson’s special vow, and his strength came from Jehovah’s spirit — not from outward ritual perfection. His contacts with dead bodies were incidental to the work Jehovah himself assigned: a lion he had killed, the gates of Gaza, Philistines he had struck down in battle. Jehovah, who instituted the vow, continued to empower him, because Samson’s heart was still dedicated to his God. The account reminds us that Jehovah weighs the heart and the circumstances — he is not a pedantic accountant of technicalities.

cbs.label: Dig Deeper · 2
cbs.q: What shows that Samson needed God’s holy spirit to carry the doors and the side posts from Gaza to Hebron? (w04 10/15 15 ¶¶7-8) Picture A
cbs.answer: The city gate of a fortified city was a massive structure — heavy doors, two side posts and a bar, built to withstand assault. A strong man might push such a gate open; no man carries the whole assembly on his shoulders some 60 kilometers uphill to Hebron in a single night. That feat took the same power that earlier enabled Samson to tear a lion in two and to break fresh ropes. “He put them on his shoulders and carried them up to the top of the mountain that faces Hebʹron.” (Judg. 16:3)

scriptures.quote: However, Samson kept lying there until midnight. Then he got up at midnight and grabbed the doors of the city gate and the two side posts and pulled them out along with the bar. He put them on his shoulders and carried them up to the top of the mountain that faces Hebʹron.

cbs.label: Dig Deeper · 3
cbs.q: What indicates that Delilah might have been an Israelite? (w05 3/15 28 ¶3)
cbs.answer: The valley of Sorek, where Delilah lived, lay in the border region between Philistine and Israelite territory. Her name, too, appears to be Hebrew in origin. The Philistine lords may have chosen a woman from that border region precisely because she could get close to Samson where a Philistine woman might have aroused suspicion. If Delilah was indeed an Israelite, her treachery is sadder still: one of the covenant people selling God’s champion to his enemies for money.

cbs.label: Dig Deeper · 4
cbs.q: Why did Samson pray to take revenge for only “one of [his] two eyes”? (Judg. 16:28; it “Samson” ¶10)
cbs.answer: Notice what Samson did not ask for: not his sight back, not his freedom, not even the full score settled — only “one of my two eyes.” “Samson now called out to Jehovah: ‘Sovereign Lord Jehovah, remember me, please, and strengthen me, please, just this once, O God, and let me take revenge on the Phi·lisʹtines for one of my two eyes.’” (Judg. 16:28) His request was modest — strength, just once, to see Jehovah’s enemies humbled. Knowing he had forfeited everything by his own course, he left the outcome entirely in Jehovah’s hands.

scriptures.quote: Samson now called out to Jehovah: “Sovereign Lord Jehovah, remember me, please, and strengthen me, please, just this once, O God, and let me take revenge on the Phi·lisʹtines for one of my two eyes.”

cbs.label: Reflect · A
cbs.q: Under pressure, Samson revealed confidential information to Delilah. What can elders and their wives learn from this? (Picture B)
cbs.answer: Delilah did not storm the secret out of Samson with threats — she wore him down, day after day, with insistent pressure and appeals to his feelings. Confidential matters that an elder and his wife handle — shepherding details, the personal weaknesses of others — must be guarded just as carefully. Under enough pressure, even strong people can let slip what they should protect. So it is wise to keep confidences safe, not to be worn down by insistent questioners — however well-meaning — and to be careful about whom we ourselves confide in.

cbs.label: Reflect · B
cbs.q: Samson made a serious mistake, but Jehovah later used him mightily. If a Christian today makes a mistake, how may the example of Samson motivate him not to give up?
cbs.answer: Samson’s failures were great — self-will, loose lips, sensual compromise. Yet the last thing the Bible records about him is a humble prayer, and Jehovah answered it mightily; Paul later listed Samson among the men of faith. If you have made a serious mistake, do not conclude that your record of service is finished. Repent sincerely, pray, and get back to serving. Jehovah reads the repentant heart, not merely the past record — and he can still use you mightily, as he used Samson at the very end.

cbs.label: Reflect · C
cbs.q: How might you imitate the courage of Samson in your life?
cbs.answer: We are not asked to fight Philistines, but courage is still needed daily: courage to identify openly with Jehovah’s people when schoolmates or workmates mock our faith; courage to keep preaching when the door slams; courage to speak the truth that could save a loved one’s life, even though it may cost his approval. And courage of Samson’s last kind — to admit our own mistakes, pray honestly, and ask Jehovah for strength “just this once” to do what is right.

cbs.label: Meditate · A
cbs.q: What does this account teach me about Jehovah?
cbs.answer: It teaches me that Jehovah sees beyond a person’s worst chapter. He did not excuse Samson’s sin — the consequences were real — but he never withdrew his willingness to hear a repentant prayer. It teaches me that Jehovah’s power does not depend on human perfection: the same spirit that empowered a flawed but dedicated Nazirite can empower me. And it teaches me that Jehovah keeps delivering his people, even choosing to do it through imperfect men whom he can trust to return to him.

cbs.label: Meditate · B
cbs.q: How does the account tie in with Jehovah’s purposes?
cbs.answer: Samson’s victories kept the Philistines from crushing Israel in the days of the judges, protecting the nation through which the promised Seed would come. Centuries later, Paul included Samson among those who “from a weak state were made powerful” — proof that Jehovah’s greatest victories are won through faith, not flawlessness. The account points forward to the final deliverance: as God’s spirit empowered Samson for a last blow against the enemy, Jehovah’s King will destroy his enemies completely and give his people lasting peace.

scriptures.quote: And what more will I say? For time will fail me if I go on to relate about Gidʹe·on, Baʹrak, Samson, Jephʹthah, David, as well as Samuel and the other prophets.
from a weak state were made powerful, became mighty in war, routed invading armies.

cbs.label: Meditate · C
cbs.q: What would I like to ask Samson in the resurrection?
cbs.answer: ‘Samson, when your hair was cut and you felt that Jehovah had left you — what kept you from despair? How did you pray in the dark, blind and mocked, surrounded by men who laughed at your God?’ And: ‘What did it feel like to know that your name would stand in Hebrews 11 among the faithful — you, with all your mistakes?’ I suspect he would smile and say: ‘Jehovah never stopped listening. Never assume that he has stopped listening to you.’

items.q: What do you learn from John’s experience? (See also pictures.)
items.comment: What impresses me about John is that thankfulness was organized. He didn’t just feel grateful — he wrote down each name, then prayed for each person by name that same day. Even at 95, frail and dependent, he stayed “very happy and contented,” as his caregiver said. It shows that a thankful attitude doesn’t depend on our circumstances; it depends on what we choose to notice — and John chose to notice kindnesses. Gratitude and happiness really do feed each other.
items.insight: John’s thankfulness was not a mood; it was a system — names recorded, prayers offered one by one. Happiness followed as a by-product of noticing, not of health or comfort.
items.apply: Tonight, write down three people who showed you kindness this week — and mention each one by name in your evening prayer.

paraNotes.points: At 95, John thanked every helper by name, wrote each name in a notebook, and prayed for each one individually that same day; his caregiver said he stayed happy and contented.
paraNotes.highlight: Footnote a: the name has been changed. And the picture is a reenactment of John’s experience — the question builds on it.

items.q: What is true of many in today’s world?
items.comment: Many feel entitled — the Bible foretold it: “critical times hard to deal with,” with people “unthankful.” (2 Tim. 3:1, 2) You see it everywhere: someone is served all day and nobody says thanks. Some simply forget to be grateful, but many honestly feel the world owes them something. It’s a selfish way of thinking, and it robs a person of joy. We have to be different — Jehovah’s worshippers must not absorb that spirit.

scriptures.quote: But know this, that in the last days critical times hard to deal with will be here. For men will be lovers of themselves, lovers of money, boastful, haughty, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, disloyal,
scriptures.use: Paul foretold that people in the last days would be unthankful — the thankless world this paragraph describes.

items.insight: “Unthankful” is not a random trait in Paul’s list — entitlement and gratitude cannot live in the same heart, and the last days breed entitlement.
items.apply: Catch yourself once this week when you start to think “I deserve …” — and turn the sentence into thanks for what you already have.

paraNotes.points: Paul foretold “critical times” marked by unthankfulness (2 Tim. 3:1, 2); many today not only forget to say thanks — they feel entitled, as if things were owed to them.
paraNotes.highlight: “Unthankful” sits in Paul’s list of last-days traits — thanklessness is a sign of the times, not just bad manners.

items.q: What will we discuss in this article?
items.comment: Paul’s words hit home: “Show yourselves thankful.” (Col. 3:15) Notice — show. Feeling grateful isn’t enough; Jehovah wants us to look for ways to express it, in word and in deed. The article walks through three questions: why should we be thankful, how do we cultivate a deep sense of gratitude, and how do we actually show ourselves thankful? By the end, I want to leave with one or two concrete things I’ll do differently this week.

scriptures.quote: Also, let the peace of the Christ rule in your hearts, for you were called to that peace in one body. And show yourselves thankful.
scriptures.use: Paul’s direct command that Jehovah’s worshippers must show themselves thankful.

items.insight: Colossians 3:15 puts thankfulness inside a command about the peace of the Christ ruling in the body — gratitude is a congregational, not just personal, virtue.
items.apply: Decide now: when the article ends, name one way you will show thankfulness this week — don’t leave with only good feelings.

paraNotes.points: God’s worshippers must be different: “Show yourselves thankful” (Col. 3:15) — feel it and express it; the article answers three questions: why be thankful, how to cultivate gratitude, how to show it.
paraNotes.highlight: The three section headings of the article are exactly those three questions — follow the outline as you listen.

items.q: Why is a thankless attitude harmful?
items.comment: A thankless attitude makes us negative, and the Bible nails it: “All the days of the afflicted one are bad.” (Prov. 15:15) We can’t always control what trial comes, but we control what we focus on. When I only rehearse what’s wrong, everything looks gloomy and joy drains away — the positive things become invisible. That’s why gratitude is protection: it keeps my eyes open to what Jehovah is doing for me even while I’m still in the trial.

scriptures.quote: All the days of the afflicted one are bad,
scriptures.use: Shows that a negative, thankless outlook makes every day seem bad.

items.insight: Negativity is not honesty — it is a filter that hides Jehovah’s kindnesses. The afflicted one’s days are “bad” partly because gloom colors everything he looks at.
items.apply: When a trial hits this week, name one positive thing each day before you dwell on the negative.

paraNotes.points: Ungrateful people tend to be negative — “All the days of the afflicted one are bad” (Prov. 15:15); we can’t control trials but we can control our response; a negative outlook blinds us to the positive and robs us of joy.

items.q: How does a thankful attitude increase our happiness?
items.comment: The second half of the verse flips it: “The one with a cheerful heart has a continual feast.” (Prov. 15:15) A cheerful heart chooses what to look at — the things to be thankful for — and the negatives fade into the background. And notice: a “continual feast” isn’t a one-time party; it’s ongoing contentment, daily nourishment. Gratitude genuinely makes us happier. It sounds simple, but it works — try it and see.

scriptures.quote: But the one with a cheerful heart has a continual feast.
scriptures.use: Shows that a thankful, cheerful heart produces ongoing contentment — “a continual feast.”

items.insight: “A continual feast” is a state of heart, not a set of circumstances — the cheerful heart dines daily on blessings the gloomy heart cannot see.
items.apply: End each evening this week by naming aloud one thing that made the day a “feast.”

paraNotes.points: Gratitude increases happiness — “The one with a cheerful heart has a continual feast” (Prov. 15:15): a thankful outlook crowds out the negative and produces ongoing contentment.

items.q: Why can it be said that expressing gratitude helps us not to “be anxious”? (Philippians 4:6, 7)
items.comment: Philippians 4:6, 7 connects thanksgiving with peace: when we pray “along with thanksgiving,” Jehovah gives “the peace of God that surpasses all understanding.” Why does it work? Because gratitude shifts my focus off tomorrow’s uncertainties and onto what Jehovah has already done for me. If he carried me this far, he can carry me one more day — exactly what Jesus meant when he said, “never be anxious about the next day.” Tearful, thankful prayers really do quiet an anxious heart.

scriptures.quote: Do not be anxious over anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication along with thanksgiving, let your petitions be made known to God; and the peace of God that surpasses all understanding will guard your hearts and your mental powers by means of Christ Jesus.
scriptures.use: Connects thanksgiving in prayer with “the peace of God” that guards the heart and mind.

scriptures.quote: So never be anxious about the next day, for the next day will have its own anxieties. Each day has enough of its own troubles.
scriptures.use: Jesus’ counsel not to be anxious about the next day, which gratitude supports.

items.insight: Thanksgiving in prayer is not decoration — it is the mechanism that re-anchors the heart to past care, which is why it produces real peace rather than wishful thinking.
items.apply: Before your next anxious prayer, recall one specific past deliverance and open the prayer with thanks for it.

paraNotes.points: Praying “along with thanksgiving” shifts the focus from tomorrow’s worries to what Jehovah has already given (Phil. 4:6, 7; Matt. 6:25-34); in response he gives “the peace of God” that eases anxiety.

items.q: How does a thankful attitude draw us closer to Jehovah? (James 1:17)
items.comment: James 1:17 says every good gift comes from Jehovah. And notice why he gives: not because we’ve earned it, but because he loves us — “By this undeserved kindness you have been saved through faith … it is God’s gift.” (Eph. 2:8) When I look at the ransom, the hope of salvation, the daily care — all undeserved — gratitude rises naturally. And gratitude draws me close to him as my Father and best Friend. You can’t feel that kind of debt and stay distant from the Giver.

scriptures.quote: Every good gift and every perfect present is from above, coming down from the Father of the celestial lights, who does not vary or change like the shifting shadows.
scriptures.use: Every good gift comes from Jehovah — the reason we are thankful.

scriptures.quote: By this undeserved kindness you have been saved through faith, and this is not of your own doing; rather, it is God’s gift.
scriptures.use: Salvation is God’s undeserved gift, given out of love — gratitude is the right response.

items.insight: Gratitude is the correct response to grace: nothing we have was owed to us, so nothing we have may be taken for granted.
items.apply: When you pray this week, thank Jehovah for one gift you have never explicitly thanked him for — perhaps the ransom itself.

paraNotes.points: Every good gift comes from Jehovah (James 1:17) — the ransom and the hope of salvation, given out of love, not merit (Rom. 3:24; Eph. 2:8); gratitude for undeserved kindness draws us close to him as beloved Father and best Friend.

items.q: How do we benefit by reflecting on past blessings? (2 Corinthians 4:7)
items.comment: Looking back changes how I see now. All of us have had that moment — a loss, a health crisis, opposition — when we wondered how we survived. Paul explains it: “we have this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the power beyond what is normal may be God’s and not from us.” (2 Cor. 4:7) It wasn’t me; it was him. Remembering that builds deep gratitude — and, honestly, confidence for the next trial: the God who carried me then hasn’t retired.

scriptures.quote: However, we have this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the power beyond what is normal may be God’s and not from us.
scriptures.use: The “power beyond what is normal” that carried us through past trials is God’s.

scriptures.quote: Let me praise Jehovah; May I never forget all that he has done.
scriptures.use: David’s resolve never to forget all Jehovah has done — the spirit of reflecting on past blessings.

items.insight: Memory is faith’s fuel: the “power beyond what is normal” is often only visible in the rearview mirror — reflection converts endurance into gratitude and confidence.
items.apply: Write down the hardest season you have passed through and one line on how Jehovah carried you — keep it for the next trial.

paraNotes.points: Reflect on past blessings: the trial you survived was carried by “the power beyond what is normal” (2 Cor. 4:7) — remembering Jehovah’s past help produces deep gratitude (Ps. 103:2).
paraNotes.highlight: The study note on “the power beyond what is normal” is worth reading — it explains that Jehovah blessed Paul’s own efforts to cope, the same way he blesses ours.

items.q: What blessings from Jehovah do you enjoy each day? (See also picture.)
items.comment: Paul’s counsel is sweeping: “Give thanks for everything.” (1 Thess. 5:18) So the list should cover both kinds of blessings. Spiritual ones — a prayer answered, a scripture that seemed written for me that morning, an article that met a need exactly. Physical ones — “life and breath” (Acts 17:25), a sunset, a good meal, a hug. David said God’s thoughts toward him were “too numerous to recount” (Ps. 40:5). A written list, like John’s, helps me see that for myself — morning or night.

scriptures.quote: Give thanks for everything. This is God’s will for you in Christ Jesus.
scriptures.use: The Bible’s sweeping command to give thanks for everything, which the daily blessings list obeys.

scriptures.quote: nor is he served by human hands as if he needed anything, because he himself gives to all people life and breath and all things.
scriptures.use: Jehovah gives us “life and breath” — the physical blessings we enjoy each day.

scriptures.quote: How many things you have done, O Jehovah my God, Your wonderful works and your thoughts toward us. None can compare to you; If I were to try to tell and speak of them, They would be too numerous to recount!
scriptures.use: David’s blessings were “too numerous to recount” — why a written list helps us count them.

items.insight: Counting blessings turns vague gratitude into evidence: “too numerous to recount” becomes convincing only when we actually start counting.
items.apply: Start a blessings list today — in the morning or at night — and keep it going for the whole week.

paraNotes.points: Count present blessings daily — in the morning to start the day or at night to end it (1 Thess. 5:18; Ps. 92:1, 2); a written list, like John’s, makes the counting concrete.
paraNotes.highlight: Picture c: on a gloomy day, a sister reflects on her blessings, including scriptures that bring her comfort — the gloomiest days are exactly when the list matters most.

paraNotes.points: Start with daily reasons: spiritual blessings (answered prayers, comforting scriptures, an article or video that met a need) and physical ones — because God gives us “life and breath” (Acts 17:25; Ps. 40:5; Eph. 5:20).
paraNotes.highlight: The paragraph closes with a question to the audience — have your own additions to the list ready to answer it.

items.q: What blessings do we receive through our brothers and sisters?
items.comment: “Look! How good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity!” (Ps. 133:1) The brotherhood is one of Jehovah’s richest gifts. Sometimes it’s a friend who “sticks closer than a brother” (Prov. 18:24); sometimes it’s a sister who simply crosses the aisle and sings the rest of a song with a grieving mother. Even small acts of kindness count as blessings. We shouldn’t wait to be the beneficiary — look for someone to bless today.

scriptures.quote: Look! How good and how pleasant it is For brothers to dwell together in unity!
scriptures.use: The blessing of brothers dwelling together in unity — part of the brotherhood’s gifts.

scriptures.quote: There are companions ready to crush one another, But there is a friend who sticks closer than a brother.
scriptures.use: A friend who sticks closer than a brother — the kindness we receive through the congregation.

items.insight: The brotherhood is designed as a delivery system for Jehovah’s kindness — through people, he comforts us in ways no private prayer could.
items.apply: Be the answer to someone’s list: do one thoughtful deed or send one encouraging word to a specific brother or sister this week.

paraNotes.points: Count the blessings of a loving, united brotherhood — unity (Ps. 133:1; Prov. 18:24), thoughtful deeds and encouraging words (Prov. 12:25; 16:24); even small acts of kindness count.
paraNotes.highlight: The experience of the grieving mother and the sister who sang the rest of the song with her — one hug turned grief into gratitude. (See also picture.)

paraNotes.points: Reflecting on blessings both past and present cultivates deep gratitude — but gratitude must also be expressed; the final section of the article shows how, in word and in deed.

items.q: How can we express our thankfulness?
items.comment: Paul shows both channels in one sentence: “do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, thanking God the Father through him” — in word or in deed. (Col. 3:17) So thankfulness has a voice and it has hands. We thank Jehovah, and he is pleased when we also thank people around us. The rest of the article gives practical suggestions for both — words first, then deeds. Let’s take them and use them this week.

scriptures.quote: Whatever it is that you do in word or in deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, thanking God the Father through him.
scriptures.use: Thankfulness is expressed both in word and in deed — everything done, thanking God through Christ.

items.insight: Thankfulness has two currencies — words and deeds — and both the recipients (Jehovah, and people) and both channels matter. Half thankfulness is no thankfulness.
items.apply: Pick one person: before Sunday, thank them in words and do something for them.

paraNotes.points: The theme text in context: “do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, thanking God the Father through him” (Col. 3:15, 17) — thankfulness is expressed both in word and in deed, to Jehovah and to others.

items.q: In what ways can you express your thankfulness to others in words? (See also pictures.)
items.comment: Say thank you — out loud, promptly, even for small kindnesses like a held door or an encouraging word. And sometimes put it in writing: a text, an email, or a letter lasts longer than a word spoken in passing. Paul asked the Thessalonians to “show respect for those who are working hard among you” (1 Thess. 5:12, 13) — that could be a written note after a shepherding call. And let’s not forget the wives who give up time with their husbands so the flock can be cared for.

scriptures.quote: Now we request you, brothers, to show respect for those who are working hard among you and presiding over you in the Lord and admonishing you; and to give them extraordinary consideration in love because of their work. Be peaceable with one another.
scriptures.use: Respect and love for those working hard among us — expressed in words of appreciation to elders.

items.insight: Written gratitude has a longer shelf life than spoken — a text or letter can be reread on the discouraging days when spoken words are forgotten.
items.apply: Send one written thank-you this week — to an elder after a shepherding call, or to the wife who serves behind the scenes.

paraNotes.points: Express thanks in words: prompt spoken thanks for small kindnesses, and written thanks where possible (1 Thess. 5:12, 13) — including elders who shepherd and their wives who sacrifice time with their husbands.
paraNotes.highlight: The picture shows practical, everyday gratitude — notice how small the gestures are. (See also pictures.)

items.q: How can we express our thankfulness to Jehovah in words?
items.comment: Above all, prayers of thanksgiving. Most of my prayers are petitions — help me, strengthen me, forgive me. But Paul speaks of “every form of prayer” (Eph. 6:18), and the psalmist invites us to “come into his presence with thanksgiving” (Ps. 95:2). The check the article suggests is piercing: in my prayers, am I mindful of thanking Jehovah for my blessings, or do I just ask him for what I need? A prayer that is all requests and no thanks is one-sided.

scriptures.quote: while with every form of prayer and supplication you carry on prayer on every occasion in spirit. And to that end stay awake, constantly making supplication in behalf of all the holy ones.
scriptures.use: Every form of prayer includes prayers of thanksgiving, not only petition.

scriptures.quote: Let us come into his presence with thanksgiving; Let us sing and shout in triumph to him.
scriptures.use: The invitation to come into Jehovah’s presence with thanksgiving.

items.insight: A prayer audit is a spiritual health check: all-petition prayers treat Jehovah as a dispenser; thanksgiving restores the relationship.
items.apply: In your midweek prayer, spend the first full minute only giving thanks — no requests.

paraNotes.points: Above all, thank Jehovah in words — heartfelt prayers of thanksgiving, not only petition and supplication (Eph. 6:18; Ps. 95:2).
paraNotes.highlight: The self-check question: ‘In my prayers, am I mindful of thanking Jehovah for my blessings or do I just ask him for what I need?’

items.q: Why should we express our thankfulness to others in deeds?
items.comment: Jesus’ words: “There is more happiness in giving than there is in receiving.” (Acts 20:35) When someone’s kindness touches my heart, doing something in return completes the circle. It brings that greater happiness — giving feels better than getting — and it makes the other person feel appreciated and valued, which strengthens the bond between us. Gratitude that stays in my head helps no one; gratitude that acts encourages the giver and deepens the friendship.

scriptures.quote: “There is more happiness in giving than there is in receiving.”
scriptures.use: Jesus’ words: there is more happiness in giving — the greater happiness of gratitude expressed in deeds.

items.insight: Deeds of gratitude complete the circuit — the giver feels valued, the bond strengthens, and the greater happiness of giving is honored on both sides.
items.apply: Return a kindness this week in action — cook, visit, repair, drive — not just words.

paraNotes.points: Express thanks in deeds to others: acting on gratitude brings “the greater happiness that comes from giving” (Acts 20:35) and makes others feel appreciated and valued, strengthening the bond.

items.q: How can we express our thankfulness to Jehovah in deeds? (Romans 12:1)
items.comment: The deepest answer to Jehovah’s gifts is to give ourselves back to him: “present your bodies as a living sacrifice.” (Rom. 12:1) That began with our dedication and baptism, and it continues — giving of our time, energy and material resources in sacred service: daily Bible reading and meditation, sharing the good news, regular and active meeting attendance, and supporting Kingdom interests materially. And “work at it whole-souled as for Jehovah” (Col. 3:23, 24) — whole-souled service is thankfulness with our whole life attached to it.

scriptures.quote: Therefore, I appeal to you by the compassions of God, brothers, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, a sacred service with your power of reason.
scriptures.use: Presenting our bodies as a living sacrifice — the deepest way to thank Jehovah in deeds.

scriptures.quote: Whatever you are doing, work at it whole-souled as for Jehovah, and not for men, for you know that it is from Jehovah you will receive the inheritance as a reward. Slave for the Master, Christ.
scriptures.use: Working whole-souled as for Jehovah — whole-souled service expresses the depth of our thankfulness.

items.insight: “A living sacrifice” means the offering never stops: dedication is not a one-time payment but a daily renewal of everything — mind, heart, strength, time and means.
items.apply: Examine one area of service that has gone routine for you this month — and renew it deliberately as an act of thanksgiving.

paraNotes.points: The deepest thanksgiving in deeds: present ourselves to Jehovah as “a living sacrifice” (Rom. 12:1) — total dedication of mind, heart and strength, every faculty.
paraNotes.highlight: The study note on Romans 12:1 is quoted in the paragraph: dedication involves ‘every aspect of his life’ — no part is left over for ourselves.

paraNotes.points: Dedication moved us to baptism; we keep giving — time, energy, resources — through daily reading and meditation, preaching, regular meeting participation and material support (Ps. 1:2, 3; 2 Cor. 8:4; Heb. 10:24, 25; 13:15; Col. 3:23, 24).

items.q: Why are you determined to show yourself thankful?
items.comment: Because a thankful life is simply better — more happiness, less anxiety and, most of all, a closer walk with Jehovah. “Give thanks to Jehovah, for he is good” (Ps. 106:1), and “without faith it is impossible to please God well,” for he “becomes the rewarder of those earnestly seeking him.” (Heb. 11:6) I want to keep showing gratitude in word and in deed — especially to Jehovah — and trust his promise of blessings “now and forever.”

scriptures.quote: Praise Jah! Give thanks to Jehovah, for he is good; His loyal love endures forever.
scriptures.use: Jehovah is good — the standing reason to give thanks.

scriptures.quote: Moreover, without faith it is impossible to please God well, for whoever approaches God must believe that he is and that he becomes the rewarder of those earnestly seeking him.
scriptures.use: Faith pleases God; he rewards those earnestly seeking him — the grateful worshipper’s confidence.

items.insight: Gratitude is not the closing sentiment of the article; it is the posture that pleases God — the rewarder “earnestly seeking him” is the grateful one.
items.apply: Close this week the way John closed his days: names written, prayers said, thankfulness shown.

paraNotes.points: A thankful attitude increases happiness, reduces anxiety and draws us closer to Jehovah; keep showing gratitude in word and deed — especially to Jehovah — and he rewards with blessings “now and forever” (Ps. 106:1; Heb. 11:6).

recap.comment: Because every good gift comes from Jehovah, given out of love rather than merit (James 1:17; Eph. 2:8). Gratitude increases our happiness and reduces anxiety, and it draws us closer to him as our Father and Friend. A thankless attitude does the opposite — it breeds negativity and robs us of joy.

recap.q: How can you cultivate a deep sense of gratitude?
recap.comment: Reflect on past blessings — the trials Jehovah carried you through by “the power beyond what is normal” — and on present ones, counting them each day, even in writing. Include the blessings that come through the loving brotherhood. Reflection turns vague appreciation into deep, heartfelt gratitude.

recap.q: How can you show yourself thankful?
recap.comment: In word and in deed: prompt, spoken and written thanks to people — including elders, their wives and anyone showing even a small kindness — and above all heartfelt prayers of thanksgiving to Jehovah. The deepest expression is giving ourselves back to him: whole-souled sacred service, daily reading and meditation, preaching, meeting attendance and material support.

daily.comment: While on earth, Jesus perfectly cared for the work his Father had given him to do. ( John 17:4 ) But Jesus did not have the attitude, ‘If you want something done right, you must do it yourself.’ He trained others to do the work. Jesus entrusted his disciples with the responsibility of caring for Jehovah’s precious sheep and taking the lead in the preaching and teaching work. Jesus gave his disciples frank but loving counsel. Some of them had the tendency to doubt, so he counseled them. ( Luke 24:25-27; John 20:27 ) He drove home the need for them to put greater emphasis on the shepherding work than on their secular careers. ( John 21:15 ) He reminded them not to become unduly concerned about what privileges others might receive. ( John 21:20-22 ) And he corrected some wrong ideas they had about the Kingdom and helped them focus on getting the good news preached.— Acts 1:6-8 . w24.10 15-16 ¶13-14 December 7-13

daily.scripture: The righteous will possess the earth, and they will live forever on it.
daily.comment: Obedience leads to life. Like the Israelites who were on the threshold of the Promised Land, we are on the verge of entering God’s promised new world, where we will see the earth transformed into a paradise. ( Isa. 35:1; Luke 23:43 ) The Devil and his demons will be gone. ( Rev. 20:2, 3 ) No longer will false religion lead people away from Jehovah. ( Rev. 17:16 ) No longer will human governments oppress those under their care. ( Rev. 19:19, 20 ) Paradise will have no place for rebels. ( Ps. 37:10, 11 ) People everywhere will obey Jehovah’s righteous laws, which promote unity and peace. Thus, they will love and trust one another. ( Isa. 11:9 ) What a wonderful prospect! What is more, if we obey Jehovah, we can continue to live on a paradise earth not just for hundreds of years but for all eternity.— John 3:16 . w24.11 9 ¶7 December 7-13

daily.scripture: This good news of the Kingdom will be preached in all the inhabited earth for a witness to all the nations.
daily.comment: The prophecy in today’s text is being fulfilled in our day as never before. The Kingdom message is published in more than 1,000 languages, and by means of the jw.org website, it is available to the majority of the world’s population. However, Jesus also told his disciples that they would not “complete the circuit of the cities,” or preach to everyone, before he would come. ( Matt. 10:23; 25:31-33 ) Jesus’ words will prove to be true in our day as well. Millions of people today live in areas where the preaching work is severely restricted. In addition, hundreds of babies are born every minute. We do our best to reach people from “every nation and tribe and tongue” with the good news. ( Rev. 14:6 ) But the fact is that we will not be able to share the good news with each individual on earth before the end comes. w24.05 10 ¶6-7 December 7-13

daily.scripture: They are no longer two, but one flesh.
daily.comment: Jesus used his words to comfort and refresh others. He did not speak harshly to his followers. ( Luke 8:47, 48 ) What an excellent example for Christian husbands! Jesus instructed husbands to remain loyal to their wife. He quoted his Father, who said that a husband should “stick to his wife.” ( Matt. 19:4-6 ) The Greek verb used in that passage for “stick to” literally means “to glue.” Therefore, the marital bond between a husband and a wife should be so strong that it is as if they were glued together. Their bond cannot be broken without damaging both of them. A husband who develops such a bond with his wife will reject all forms of pornography. He will immediately turn away from “looking at what is worthless.” ( Ps. 119:37 ) In effect, he makes a contract with his eyes not to look passionately at any woman other than his wife.— Job 31:1 . w25.01 10 ¶12-13 December 7-13

daily.scripture: Our God . . . will forgive in a large way.
daily.comment: The forgiveness humans extend can be complicated. The way Jehovah forgives us imperfect humans is very different from the way we forgive one another. The forgiveness Jehovah extends is unique. The psalmist said of Jehovah: “With you there is true forgiveness, so that you may be held in awe.” ( Ps. 130:4 ) Yes, Jehovah’s forgiveness is “true forgiveness.” He sets the ultimate standard of what forgiveness really means. In some cases, Bible writers used a Hebrew word for forgiveness that is never used to describe human forgiveness. When Jehovah forgives someone, that person’s sin is wiped out. The damaged relationship is entirely restored. Jehovah’s forgiveness is amazingly complete and generous. w25.02 8 ¶1-3 December 7-13

daily.scripture: He ordered us to preach to the people and to give a thorough witness.
daily.comment: Our success in the ministry does not depend on the results we obtain. Why? Because we have done what Jehovah and his Son want us to do—we have given a witness. Even when we do not find anyone to speak with or when our message is rejected, we can have joy because we know that we are pleasing our heavenly Father. ( Prov. 27:11 ) We can also rejoice when another publisher finds an interested person in the territory. The Watchtower has likened our work to searching for a lost child. Many are involved in looking for him, covering one area after another. When the child is found, everyone—not just the individual who found him—​has reason to rejoice. Similarly, the disciple-making work is a team effort. All are needed to cover the territory, and all rejoice when a new one starts attending meetings. w24.04 18 ¶13-14 December 7-13

daily.scripture: All those who were rightly disposed for everlasting life became believers.
daily.comment: What exciting prospects lie ahead of us! With Jehovah’s blessing, we hope to see many more accept the truth before the great tribulation begins. Also, we are thrilled at the possibility that even during the great tribulation, we may see still more people turn away from Satan’s dying world and join us in praising Jehovah! Meanwhile, we have work to do. We have the privilege of sharing in a never-to-be-repeated proclamation—the preaching of the good news of God’s Kingdom throughout the earth. At the same time, we must keep sounding the warning. People need to know that the end of this wicked system of things is rapidly approaching. Motivated by love—love for the good news, love for people and, above all, love for Jehovah God and his name—​we will keep preaching with eagerness, urgency, and zeal until Jehovah says, “It is enough!” w24.05 19 ¶14-16 December 7-13
